title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI-generated fake news article impersonated real people, the Reserve Bank governor and a finance presenter, to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The article was a text-based fabrication designed to look like journalism, not a deepfake video. This kind of impersonation scam requires no consent from the people being impersonated and depends on readers not verifying the sources they encounter.

The failure was in deployment: scammers used AI systems to generate false content at scale and distributed it where people making investment decisions would encounter it. A reader who wanted to verify the story could have checked whether the interview had occurred, whether the platform was licensed, or whether the quoted officials had made public statements. Whether this required blocking such content at the point of generation, at the point of distribution, or catching it only when someone reported it is not established.

It is not established whether the AI systems used were purpose-built for fraud or whether they were general-purpose systems misused by scammers after deployment.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featuring Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler has emerged as part of a rising scam trend. The fabricated interview portrayed Bullock becoming upset with Kohler over questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article was designed to promote fraudulent investment opportunities, with no such interview actually occurring. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows that AI-generated deepfakes and fake investment scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated and common.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politicians, financial experts, and businesspeople including Alan Kohler, Gina Rinehart, and Dick Smith are frequently impersonated in these schemes. Scammers typically create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, and advertisements to lure victims into providing personal details. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing. Presenter Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content and the AI companies creating deepfakes should face substantial penalties.
